title: B-R-K
hook: bracha (blessing), berech (knee), breichah (pool): blessing bends and flows

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sh-L-M: shalom, shalem, shilem, and your line: peace is wholeness. Today, the root under baruch, and the end of the week.

Evening, outside a town, at a well. A servant has walked a long way with ten camels, sent to find a wife for his master's son. Before he asks anything of anyone, he brings the camels down onto their knees beside the water. In Hebrew, the verb for making them kneel is built on bet, resh, kaf, the same three letters as baruch, the first word of a blessing. Only then does the servant pray. The root of blessing, down in the dust beside the water.
screen: `A WELL AT EVENING.` → `THE CAMELS KNEEL.` → `THE SAME LETTERS AS BARUCH.`

segments.voice: B-R-K. Four ways in. First, bracha: a blessing. Baruch, blessed, from three days ago, grows from these letters. Second, berech: a knee. In Psalm 95, the call to worship says "let us kneel before the LORD," and the Hebrew for kneel is from this root. In the Amidah, the standing prayer, a custom traced to the Talmud has people bend the knees at baruch, bow at atah, and stand straight again for God's name. The body says the word. Third, breichah: a pool, water gathered low where the ground bends down to hold it. Dictionaries list the knee and the blessing under the same letters. Whether they began as one word is a question for linguists. But some readers hear them together: blessing is something you bend toward, and something that pools and flows. Fourth, the week behind you. It began with dots, the nikud that give letters a voice. Then your first word, shalom. Then the Shema's first two words, a silent eye and a dot that moved. Then baruch atah. Then shoresh, the root under the word, and the first root, sh-l-m, peace as wholeness. And now b-r-k, the root under the blessing you learned to read. A week ago these were single letters. Now they're words you can sound out, and roots you can dig up.
screen: `BRACHA: A BLESSING.` · `BERECH: THE KNEE THAT BENDS.` · `BREICHAH: WATER GATHERED LOW.` · `THE WEEK: DOTS, WORDS, ROOTS.` · then, large: `BLESSING BENDS.`

segments.voice: If you're able, stand; sitting is fine too. Bring to mind one thing from this week you're grateful for, small and real, and slowly let your knees bend a little, the way the custom bends at baruch, then straighten, or if you're seated, bow your head and lift it. Once is enough; then sit and let the thanks pool, and if you pray, you can say baruch atah as you bend.
B-R-K. Bet, resh, kaf: the root of bracha, blessing, sitting beside berech, knee, and breichah, pool. Today's word.
Your line: blessing bends. Thanks can gather low, like water. That's a week of reading.

howItsDone: In the Amidah, worshippers bend the knees at the word baruch, bow at atah, and straighten before God's name; the Hebrew words for blessing and knee are listed under the same three letters, b-r-k.

chat.says: Why do some people bend their knees during the Amidah?
options: Baruch shares a root with berech, knee: people bend at baruch, bow at atah, then straighten.
It's to rest tired legs halfway through, since the whole Amidah is said standing.
They bend to show sorrow for sins; the knee bend is only done on fast days.
chat.meaning: B-R-K gives both bracha, blessing, and berech, knee; a custom traced to the Talmud bends the knees at baruch in the Amidah.

notes: Psalms 95:6 fragment quoted as JPS 1917 (KJV has the same words); nivrechah from B-R-K. Confirm.
Genesis 24:10–11 paraphrased: Abraham's servant, ten camels (the count is in Genesis 24:10), makes them kneel (vayavrech) by the well at evening; then prays (24:12). Confirm.
Amidah bowing custom traced to Berakhot 12a–b (bow at baruch, straighten at the Name); the knee-bend at baruch and bow at atah are the common practice. Confirm the source and phrasing.
Whether bracha and berech are etymologically one root is left open on purpose ('a question for linguists'). Script says 'some readers hear them together'.
Breichah: e.g. 2 Kings 20:20; not cited in the voice. Confirm gloss 'pool'.
